results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database. According to VFB, the mushroom body is divided into these three parts: the calyx, which receives sensory interneuron afferents; the pedunculus, a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes; and the mushroom body lobe system, which consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch with different structures at different life stages. VFB holds various data related to the mushroom body, including images, neurons with parts in the mushroom body, and parts of the mushroom body itself, with [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of mushroom body") subclasses of mushroom body and [176](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of mushroom body") parts of mushroom body annotated.

Additionally, VFB records show that projection neurons from the antennal lobe, such as [larval antennal lobe multiglomerular projection neuron C2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111716 "Open larval antennal lobe multiglomerular projection neuron C2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), also provide input to the mushroom body. results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The LPLC2 visual neuron type is known to have specific characteristics and functions. According to VFB, the cell body of LPLC2 lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind. It has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, allowing it to detect looming stimuli. In the lobula, its main dendritic arbors are in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4. The arbors of LPLC2 span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells. LPLC2 projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. Its activity elicits a jump escape response. VFB records show that there are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe and they are cholinergic. 

VFB does not currently hold detailed connectivity data for LPLC2 beyond its projection to the PVLP. For more information on the connections of LPLC2, follow-up queries can be made to explore its presynaptic and postsynaptic partners.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, with a unique anatomy and connectivity profile. According to VFB, it can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective. The neuron enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle and descends on the ipsilateral side. It has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons. 

VFB holds various data related to the giant fiber neuron, including [23](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01, [5](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,SplitsTargeting "Run in VFB: Splits targeting DNp01") splits targeting DNp01, and [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01. Additionally, VFB has annotated [389](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") downstream connectivity classes and [472](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") upstream connectivity classes for DNp01.

Available driver lines for the giant fiber neuron include P{R48A11-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R30C01-p65.AD} and P{R68A06-GAL4.DBD} ∩ P{R25C08-p65.AD}. Relevant publications that provide more information on the giant fiber neuron include Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), and Namiki et al. (2018). 

The connectome data indicates that the giant fiber neuron has a complex connectivity profile, with both upstream and downstream connections. VFB records show that the neuron receives input from various sources, including zone A and B Johnston organ neurons, and sends output to multiple targets. 

To further explore the giant fiber neuron, you can examine the available images, splits, and transgene expression data in VFB, or investigate the upstream and downstream connectivity classes to gain a deeper understanding of its role in the Drosophila nervous system.
